opus-5.5.text:
I don't think it has to be strictly sequential. The five-level framing from OpenAI, chatbots, reasoners, agents, innovators, organizations, is a useful way to tell a story, but it makes the progression sound more linear than it really is.

My own background is in multi-agent reinforcement learning, so I've thought about the "organization" level for a long time, even before large language models. One thing you learn from multi-agent systems is that collective capability doesn't need every individual to be brilliant. Look at an ant colony, or a human company. Most people in a company aren't doing Nobel-level creative work, yet the organization can accomplish things no single person could. Coordination, division of labor, communication protocols, incentive design: these are somewhat orthogonal to individual creativity.

So in principle you could build a fairly capable AI organization out of level-three agents. Many agents, each reliably executing tasks, with good structure around them: one plans, one writes code, one tests, one reviews. We're already seeing early versions of this. Whether that counts as "level five" depends on your definition, but the organizational capability itself doesn't wait for creativity.

There's a flip side, though. If what you mean by level five is an AI organization that can run an entire company, adapting to new markets, inventing new products, handling situations nobody has seen before, then the bottleneck isn't coordination, it's open-ended problem solving. An organization of agents that can only execute well-specified tasks will get stuck the moment something truly novel happens. Somewhere in the system you need the ability to generate new hypotheses, explore, and recover from failures that aren't in the training distribution. That's much closer to what people mean by level-four creativity.

So my view is that the two will likely develop in parallel and reinforce each other. Multi-agent structure may even be one route to creativity. Diversity among agents, debate, self-play, population-based exploration: in RL we've seen many times that a population of agents discovers strategies a single agent never finds. AlphaStar's league training is an example. Creativity may partly emerge from organization rather than being a prerequisite for it.

Practically, I think the hardest problems right now are still at level three: making a single agent reliable over long horizons, with good memory, good error recovery, and the ability to learn from interaction. Without a solid level three, both creativity and organization are built on sand. So for researchers today, I'd focus on long-horizon RL for agents, and treat multi-agent organization as something that grows naturally on top of that, not something that must wait in line behind creativity.

r001.rationale: It says a capable AI organization could be built from level-three agents and that organizational capability need not wait for creativity.

r002.rationale: It discusses coordination and agent interactions, but describes organization as having structure, protocols, and incentive design; it does not propose that interactions alone create an organization without deliberate design.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think the ordering is strict. The five-level framing is useful as a map, but it treats capability as a single ladder, and I think "organizations" and "creativity" are really two different axes.

Level four, as OpenAI frames it, is about an AI that can produce genuinely new ideas, a scientist that can discover something no one has discovered before. Level five is about many agents coordinating, dividing labor, and running something the size of a company. The second one is fundamentally a systems and coordination problem. You can imagine a very large team of agents, each of which is roughly a competent engineer or analyst with limited originality, that still does a tremendous amount of useful work as an organization. Human companies are a bit like this already. Most of the people in a large firm are not doing anything that would count as level-four creativity on a given day, and the firm works because of process, memory, incentives, and communication.

So I'd say the honest answer is that organization-level AI could arrive before we have a convincing AI scientist, at least in narrow domains. We're already seeing early versions of this with multi-agent coding systems, where you have planners, implementers, reviewers, and testers working in a loop. None of them is especially creative, but the aggregate is more capable than a single model running one prompt.

That said, there's an important caveat. The reason organizations exist at all is that no individual can hold everything. If you get a model that's genuinely creative and has very long context and persistence, a lot of the "organization" collapses back into one agent with good tools. So the two levels may end up being substitutes, not just sequential steps. Whether you need a level-five organization depends a lot on how far a single level-four agent can go.

The part I think is actually hard, and where my own research interest lies, is the coordination problem itself: how agents communicate, when they trust each other, how they handle disagreement and errors that compound. Those problems don't get solved by making each agent smarter. In reinforcement learning we saw this over and over. You could have a very strong single-agent policy and the moment you put multiple copies together, you get instability, miscommunication, and emergent behavior nobody designed. So I'd reframe the question: rather than asking whether five comes after four, ask what new science is needed for five that four doesn't give you for free. I think the answer is quite a lot.

r001.rationale: The response says organization-level AI could arrive before a convincing AI scientist and describes agents with limited originality doing useful work together.

r002.rationale: The response discusses agents coordinating through roles, processes, and communication, but does not propose that their interactions could form an organization without deliberate organizational design. Its mention of undesigned emergent behavior refers to instability and miscommunication.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think they necessarily have to come in that order. Creativity is a capability of an individual system, while an organization is about how multiple systems coordinate: how they divide work, share information, check results, and make decisions. Those are related, but they’re different dimensions.

You could imagine an AI organization doing relatively routine work very effectively, without any member demonstrating extraordinary creativity. Conversely, a highly creative AI might still be poor at coordinating with others or managing a long-running project.

So I’d treat those levels as a useful framework, rather than a strict sequence. The interesting question is whether organizing AI systems can itself produce more creative outcomes. If it can, progress toward level five could help bring about level four, rather than simply waiting for it.

r001.rationale: It says an AI organization could perform routine work effectively without any member demonstrating extraordinary creativity.

r002.rationale: It describes how systems might coordinate, but does not say that interactions could create an organization without deliberate organizational design.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think it has to be a strict sequence. If level four means an AI can create genuinely new ideas, and level five means AIs can organize and work together, then those are related capabilities, but one doesn’t necessarily have to be completed before the other begins.

An organization can accomplish things that none of its individual members could accomplish alone. You can imagine several AI systems with limited creativity producing something much more creative through discussion, experimentation, and criticism. In that sense, organization could actually help bring about level-four creativity.

But there’s an important distinction between assembling a group of agents and building an organization that really works. Can they divide responsibilities, resolve disagreements, recognize mistakes, and stay focused on a shared goal? Simply adding more agents doesn’t solve those problems.

So I would see these levels as interacting, rather than as a staircase. Creativity makes AI organizations more powerful, and effective organization can make the whole system more creative.

r001.rationale: The response says agents with limited creativity could organize and that organization could help bring about level-four creativity, indicating an organization could exist before AI has achieved that level.

r002.rationale: It describes agent interaction as a way to increase creativity, but does not say those interactions could create an organization without deliberate organizational design.
